0.1 What this handbook is

This handbook sets up a professional cybersecurity services department inside VEL Software Solutions. It tells every employee what the department does, who may do what, how beginners are trained, and how a client engagement runs from first call to handover. It is written for people who start with basic IT knowledge and must become safe, effective defenders.

It is delivered one module at a time, because quality and legal safety matter more than speed. This first module contains the six items needed before any security work begins.

0.2 What is in Module 1 (this edition)

0.3 How to use it

  1. Read Part 3 (Authorised Testing Policy) and sign the acknowledgement before touching any tool.
  2. Follow Part 4 for your first week, then the 90-day roadmap in Part 5.
  3. Check Part 2 to learn what you may do alone, what needs approval, and what you must never do.
  4. When a client project starts, work through the stages in Part 7 in order and do not skip a gate.
  5. If you are unsure, stop and ask your Security Lead. Stopping is never a mistake; guessing about authorisation is.

0.4 The twelve golden rules

  1. No written authorisation, no testing. Verbal permission, a friendly email, or "it is our own client's website" is not authorisation.
  2. Stay inside the scope. Only the exact targets, methods and time window written in the Rules of Engagement.
  3. Practise only in owned or intentionally vulnerable labs. Learning never happens on real third-party systems.
  4. Beginners do not perform high-risk testing alone and never approve their own critical findings.
  5. Do no harm. Prefer the least intrusive method that answers the question. Back up before changing anything.
  6. Stop first, explain later if something unexpected happens: an outage, real customer data, signs of a real attacker.
  7. Verify before you report. A scanner alert is a lead, not a finding.
  8. Protect evidence and client data. Encrypt it, minimise it, never put it in an ordinary Git repository.
  9. Tell the truth in reports. No exaggeration, no hidden limitations, no invented certainty.
  10. Never claim what we do not hold. No certification, audit authority, "guaranteed secure", 24/7 SOC or structural-style safety claims we cannot back up.
  11. Never make legal decisions. Breach notification and legal interpretation belong to the client and qualified legal or compliance specialists.
  12. Write it down. If it is not in a ticket, a log or a document, it did not happen.
Important legal notice

This handbook is an internal operating procedure, not legal advice. Laws on computer misuse, data protection and incident reporting differ by country and change over time. The department must confirm applicable requirements with qualified legal counsel (for India this includes the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and CERT-In directions) before offering services or signing client contracts. Items marked "suggested default" are proposals for management approval.

Claims policy

VEL does not claim certification, independent-audit authority, accreditation, or 24/7 monitoring unless the company and named personnel actually hold the credentials and have the staffing and systems to deliver. Every proposal, website line and report must be checked against this rule by the Security Lead.

Part 1 — Department Charter and Service Portfolio

1.1 Mission and operating principles

Mission: help clients find, understand and reduce security risk through authorised, documented, defensive security work, delivered by well-trained people working under qualified supervision.

PrincipleWhat it means in daily work
Authorised onlyEvery test, scan and access has a signed authorisation and a defined scope.
Defensive purposeWe find weaknesses so they can be fixed. We do not build or deploy attack tools against third parties.
Least intrusive methodConfiguration review before scanning; scanning before manual verification; manual verification only where safe.
Supervised growthAuthority is earned through training, assessment and observed practice (the authority ladder in Part 2).
Evidence-basedFindings are confirmed, reproducible within scope, and backed by sanitised evidence.
Honest limitsReports state what was and was not tested, and what we cannot conclude.
Client data is sacredMinimise, encrypt, restrict, retain only as agreed, then securely delete.

1.2 Service portfolio

Services are grouped A to F. A service may be sold only when the delivering team has the trained people, tools and approvals listed in Part 2 and Part 3.

CategoryServicesDelivery notes and limits
A. Security AssessmentWebsite, web application, API, cloud configuration, network and infrastructure assessments; vulnerability assessment; security posture assessmentWritten authorisation and agreed rules of engagement first. Findings verified manually where safe. Report states limitations.
B. Security HardeningLinux and Windows server hardening; cloud hardening; database security; firewall configuration; IAM; MFA; secure configuration managementBack up configuration first; test in staging; change approved by client owner; rollback plan written.
C. Application SecuritySecure code review; OWASP Top 10 assessment; authentication, authorisation and session reviews; dependency scanning; SAST; DAST; software composition analysisDAST against staging by default. Production testing needs separate approval (Tier 2 or higher, Part 3).
D. Cloud SecurityAWS, Azure and GCP assessments; IAM review; storage and network security; secrets management; audit logging; compliance readinessRead-only audit roles. We never ask for owner or root credentials. "Readiness" is not certification.
E. Managed SecurityContinuous monitoring, vulnerability and patch management, security alerts, configuration reviews, incident response support, reportingDefined hours, alert volumes and response targets in contract. No 24/7 SOC claim without staffing and systems to deliver it.
F. Governance & ComplianceSecurity policies, risk registers, asset inventories, access reviews, vendor assessments, audit preparation, ISO 27001 readiness, privacy process support"Readiness support" only. VEL does not certify, and does not act as an independent auditor unless properly accredited.

1.3 What we will not do

  • Scan, test, log in to, or probe any system we do not have written authority to test.
  • Run credential attacks, malware deployment, denial-of-service, social engineering or physical intrusion unless management has formally added that service (with legal and insurance review) and the client has authorised that exact activity in writing (Tier 3).
  • Access, copy or keep more client data than the assessment needs.
  • Sell "guaranteed secure" or "unhackable" outcomes. No assessment proves the absence of vulnerabilities.
  • Make legal decisions, including whether a breach must be notified to a regulator.

A beginner (A0 or A1) must never independently perform high-risk security testing and must never approve their own critical findings. Critical and High findings need a second person (Consultant or Security Lead) to confirm before the client sees them.

2.5 Separation of duties

  • Authors do not approve their own Critical or High findings or reports.
  • The person who performs a hardening change is not the sole verifier of that change.
  • Access to client evidence is granted per engagement, reviewed monthly, and removed at close-out.
  • Administrative access to VEL's evidence store is held by the Security Lead and one named deputy only.

Part 3 — Authorised Testing Policy (POL-SEC-001)

Policy IDPOL-SEC-001 · Version 1.0 · effective on management approval
Applies toAll VEL employees, contractors and trainees who perform or support security assessment, scanning, testing, hardening or monitoring
Policy ownerSecurity Lead · approved by Founder
Breach of policyMay result in disciplinary action, termination and legal liability. Unauthorised access to computer systems can be a criminal offence.
The one-sentence policy

We test, scan or access only systems that the owner has authorised in writing, only the targets, methods and times named in that authorisation, and only by people whose authority level permits the activity.

3.1 Purpose and principles

  1. Legality: security testing without permission can break criminal and civil law, even with good intentions.
  2. Safety: testing can slow, crash or corrupt systems and expose personal data. The client's business comes first.
  3. Proportionality: use the least intrusive method that answers the question.
  4. Accountability: every action can be traced to a person, an approval and a record.

3.2 Definitions

TermMeaning
Authorised testingTesting covered by a signed agreement, asset ownership confirmation and written test authorisation naming exact scope, methods and window.
Scope / in-scopeThe exact systems (identifiers) listed in approved-targets.csv. Anything not listed is out of scope.
Rules of Engagement (RoE)The signed document that states permitted methods, exclusions, time window, contacts and stop-work conditions.
Owned labA VEL-owned, network-isolated environment built for training (for example Part 9). Includes intentionally vulnerable applications run locally.
Stop-work conditionAn event that halts all testing immediately until the Security Lead and client contact agree to resume.
Production / stagingThe live system real users depend on / a safe copy used for trials. Staging is preferred for anything active.

3.3 Mandatory preconditions (the "no-go until" list)

No scan, probe, login or test of a client system may start until every item is complete and filed. The QA Reviewer checks the pack before the Security Lead releases the "Authorised to start" marker.

ItemRequirement
☐1. Signed agreementMSA/SoW signed by an authorised signatory of the client; confidentiality and data handling terms included.
☐2. Asset ownership confirmationClient confirms in writing that it owns or has authority to authorise testing of every target. Third-party hosting, SaaS, cloud and managed providers: their testing rules are checked and, where needed, their permission obtained.
☐3. Written testing authorisationNames VEL, named testers, purpose and duration; signed and dated.
☐4. Exact target scopeDomains, IPs/ranges, applications, API endpoints, cloud account IDs, environments: no wildcards without written agreement.
☐5. Permitted test methodsListed by tier (3.5). Anything not listed is not permitted.
☐6. Excluded systemsSystems, data, networks and methods that are off-limits (e.g. payment processors, safety-critical systems, third-party SaaS).
☐7. Testing time windowStart/end date and time with time zone; blackout periods (month-end, sales events).
☐8. Emergency contact24-hour reachable named client contact with phone number, plus VEL on-call lead.
☐9. Stop-work conditionsAgreed list (3.8) and who can invoke it.
☐10. Data handling agreementWhat data may be viewed, copied, stored, where, for how long; how it is deleted; who may access it.
☐11. Backups and rollbackClient confirms current backups for any system to be changed; rollback plan agreed.
☐12. Tester authority checkEach tester's authority level (A0–A3) covers the tiers approved.

3.4 Testing is not allowed if…

  • the target is not on the approved list, even if it "looks like" the client's;
  • the authorisation is expired, unsigned, or signed by someone without authority over the asset;
  • the target is run by a third party who has not agreed (cloud provider rules, SaaS vendors, shared hosting neighbours);
  • a stop-work condition is active; or
  • you are unsure. Uncertainty is a stop, not a green light.

3.5 Risk tiers of testing activity

TierExamples (all in-scope and authorised)Minimum authorityExtra approval
T0 PassiveDocument and policy review; architecture review; reviewing client-provided exports, configs, diagrams, logs (sanitised)A1 (supervised)None beyond authorisation pack
T1 Low-impact activeSAST and dependency/secret scanning on provided code; image scanning; read-only cloud configuration audit using a read-only role; TLS/header checks of in-scope sites; authenticated read-only configuration checksA1 (senior present) / A2 independentConsultant confirms tool settings before run
T2 Moderate activeNetwork vulnerability scanning in agreed window; DAST/web scanning of staging; authenticated application testing with test accounts; manual verification of a scanner finding when safeA2Written approval from Security Lead per window; client notified; rate limits set; monitoring contact on call
T3 High riskTesting in production with active scanning; verification that could alter data or availability; anything involving credentials against live systems; social-engineering or physical elements; load or stress effectsA3 only; never traineesWritten client authorisation naming the exact activity, Security Lead + management approval, legal advice on file, enabled service
ProhibitedDenial-of-service, malware deployment, credential attacks on third parties, data exfiltration beyond minimal proof, persistence, pivoting outside scope, testing of unconfirmed ownersNobodyNot offered by the department

3.6 Mandatory safe-testing practice

  1. Re-read the RoE at the start of each session; confirm the date, window and target list.
  2. Verify the target against approved-targets.csv; check IP/domain ownership before running a tool. DNS can change.
  3. Choose the gentlest tool setting. Set rate limits and thread counts; exclude dangerous checks (e.g. destructive or denial-of-service plugins).
  4. Use a recorded, approved workstation (Stage 07): encrypted disk, MFA, logging, tool versions recorded.
  5. Log every run: who, what, command/settings, target, start/end time, result file name.
  6. Verify manually only where safe and permitted; stop at the minimum proof needed. Do not read, copy or modify real customer data beyond what the RoE allows.
  7. Handle credentials correctly: use test accounts; store in the approved password manager; never reuse; never place in tickets, chats or repositories.
  8. Report promptly: a Critical finding that is actively exploitable or exposes personal data is reported to the Security Lead immediately, then to the client contact the same day through the agreed channel.
  9. Clean up: remove test accounts, uploaded files and scan artefacts as agreed; confirm in writing.

3.7 Prohibited actions (regardless of who asks)

Never
✗Test a system for "practice" or "to impress" without written authority, including your former employer, friends' sites, public bug-bounty targets outside their published programme rules, or government/critical infrastructure.
✗Run unreviewed scripts, exploits or tools downloaded from the internet on a client system or on the company network.
✗Guess, brute-force or reuse passwords on accounts you were not given for the test.
✗Deploy malware, backdoors or persistence mechanisms on any client system.
✗Access, download or share real customer personal data beyond the minimum evidence agreed.
✗Exceed the time window, rate limits or methods in the RoE; or continue after a stop-work call.
✗Disclose vulnerabilities to anyone but the authorised client contacts and VEL's named reviewers.
✗Commit evidence, passwords, tokens, client data or exploitable detail to an ordinary Git repository, personal drive, messaging app or AI chat tool.

3.8 Stop-work conditions

Stop all active testing at once (do not "just finish this one request"), preserve notes, and call the Security Lead. The Security Lead informs the client's emergency contact.

  • Target slows, errors, or becomes unavailable during testing.
  • You discover a target not on the list, or the owner of a target is not the client.
  • You encounter personal, financial or health data not covered by the data handling agreement.
  • You find signs of a real attack or prior compromise (unknown accounts, unexpected processes, webshells).
  • The client contact or VEL lead calls stop, or the time window ends.
  • A tool behaves unexpectedly (sends traffic you did not intend).
  • A legal, safety or contractual doubt arises.

3.9 Evidence and data handling

  • Collect the minimum evidence that proves the issue: sanitised screenshots, truncated logs, configuration excerpts. Mask secrets, tokens and personal data.
  • Store evidence only in the approved, access-controlled, encrypted store. Record a SHA-256 hash and collection time for important items.
  • Retain and delete according to the signed data handling agreement and policies/retention.md; record deletion.
  • Reports for executives must not contain unnecessary exploit detail. Technical detail goes in a restricted annex with need-to-know access.

3.10 Training and lab rule

All practice for learning, tool testing or demonstrations uses owned or intentionally vulnerable environments, built on an isolated network (Part 9), with a signed Lab Authorisation Record (Appendix C). Intentionally vulnerable apps (for example OWASP Juice Shop) are run locally and never exposed to the internet or company LAN. Training skills are never tried on "real" targets.

3.11 Disclosure, incidents and breach of policy

  • Vulnerabilities found are disclosed only to the client's authorised contact via the agreed secure channel.
  • Accidental out-of-scope contact (for example a mistyped IP) is reported to the Security Lead immediately, with exact time and action. Honest early reporting is protected; concealment is a serious breach.
  • Policy violations are investigated by the Security Lead and Founder. Outcomes range from retraining to dismissal and, where required, legal reporting.

3.12 Acknowledgement

I have read and understood POL-SEC-001. I will not test, scan or access any system without written authorisation, and I will stop and ask if I am unsure.

Goal: in the first week every new employee is legally briefed, equipped with a secure workstation, assigned a mentor, and able to practise safely in the isolated lab. Technical depth comes later (Part 5). Trust comes before tools.

Why legal training comes before tools

A beginner with a scanner and no legal understanding is a risk to the client, the company and themselves. No trainee receives tool access or lab credentials until the quiz and acknowledgement are on file.

4.4 Code of Ethics (sign on Day 1)

  1. I will test only with written authorisation and only inside the agreed scope.
  2. I will protect client data and evidence as if it were my own most sensitive information.
  3. I will use my skills to defend, never to harm, and I will report discoveries only to authorised contacts.
  4. I will be honest in findings, including about what I do not know or did not test.
  5. I will stop work and report if I see danger, an unexpected impact, or a doubt about authority.
  6. I will not boast about, trade in or publish vulnerabilities or client details.
  7. I will keep learning and ask for supervision when I reach the edge of my competence.
  8. I will not discriminate against, harass or intimidate colleagues, clients or the public.
  9. I will declare conflicts of interest, including any personal link to a client or target.
  10. I accept that breaches of this code may lead to dismissal and legal action.

4.7 Mentor, supervision and probation

  • Mentor: a Consultant or Engineer at A2+ who meets the trainee weekly (30 minutes), reviews work products and signs weekly progress.
  • Observer rule: trainees shadow real engagements as silent observers only after Day 30 and only if the client has been told a trainee is present.
  • Probation reviews: Day 30, 60 and 90 with Security Lead; outcome recorded as Proceed / Proceed with support plan / Extend / Stop.
  • Escalation: concerns about workload, ethics or a colleague's behaviour go to the mentor or Security Lead; retaliation is not tolerated.

Part 5 — 90-Day Training Roadmap

The roadmap takes a beginner through the seven training levels and eight practical projects in thirteen weeks. It assumes about 40 hours a week: roughly 35% learning, 45% hands-on lab, 10% documentation, 10% mentoring and review. Pass marks and times are suggested defaults for management approval.

Part 6 — Teaching Format and Module Catalogue

6.1 The 14-point teaching format

Every training module follows the same structure so learners know what to expect and reviewers know what to check.

#ElementWhat it contains
1DefinitionWhat the topic is, in one or two plain sentences
2Business purposeWhy a client or the company cares
3Threat or risk addressedWhat can go wrong without it
4PrerequisitesEarlier modules, knowledge and access needed
5Tool installationOfficial source, version to record, licence
6Safe configurationIsolation, rate limits, authorisation and legal/operational impact
7Step-by-step procedureNumbered actions with exact commands
8Expected outputWhat correct looks like
9VerificationHow to prove it worked
10Common mistakesWhere beginners go wrong
11DocumentationWhat to record, where to file it
12Practical assignmentA task in an owned/vulnerable environment
13AssessmentQuestions and a practical rubric
14Approval requirementWho must sign before the learner proceeds, and what authority results
Rule for every module

Before any tool is used, the module states its legal and operational impact: what traffic it sends, what it may break, and what authorisation it needs. Learners must be able to explain this before they are allowed to run the tool.

6.2 Sample module M-L2-04: Linux accounts, permissions and SSH hardening

M-L2-04 · Level 2 · Linux and Windows Security · Lab-only (A0)
1. DefinitionLinux controls who can log in, what they can read, write or run through accounts, groups, file permissions and the SSH remote-login service. Hardening means removing unneeded access and tightening defaults.
2. Business purposeServers hold client data and run client applications. Weak accounts or open SSH are the commonest route to unauthorised access, outage and loss of trust.
3. Threat / riskPassword guessing against SSH, shared or stale accounts, over-permissive files, privilege escalation through misconfigured sudo or setuid programmes.
4. PrerequisitesM-L1 modules on operating systems, TCP/IP and ports; legal quiz passed; lab isolation verified.
5. Tool installationBuilt into Ubuntu Server LTS: openssh-server, sudo, ufw. Record OS version (lsb_release -a) and OpenSSH version (ssh -V) in the tool register.
6. Safe configurationLab VM on host-only network only. Snapshot first. Keep a second console session open while changing SSH, so a mistake cannot lock you out.
7. Procedure
  1. Review accounts: getent passwd | awk -F: '$7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1,$7}'
  2. Find accounts with empty passwords: sudo awk -F: '($2==""){print $1}' /etc/shadow (expected: no output)
  3. Review sudo rights: sudo -l and getent group sudo
  4. Check file permissions on sensitive files: ls -l /etc/shadow /etc/ssh/sshd_config (shadow should not be world-readable)
  5. List setuid files to understand them (read-only): sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -ls 2>/dev/null
  6. Create the SSH hardening drop-in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-vel-hardening.conf as in Part 9, step H3.
  7. Validate syntax before applying: sudo sshd -t (no output means valid), then sudo systemctl reload ssh
8. Expected outputsudo sshd -T shows permitrootlogin no, passwordauthentication no, maxauthtries 3; key login works; password login is refused.
9. VerificationFrom the analyst VM: ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no labadmin@<lab-ip> must return Permission denied (publickey). Check /var/log/auth.log for the attempt.
10. Common mistakesDisabling password login before a key works; editing the main file when an included file overrides it (first value wins); forgetting sshd -t; closing the only session.
11. DocumentationChange log (what, why, before/after), command output excerpts, rollback steps, tool register entry.
12. Practical assignmentHarden SSH on a fresh lab VM, then restore the snapshot and repeat from your own notes without the guide.
13. AssessmentFive written questions (why disable root login? what is "first value wins"? what does sshd -t do?); practical rubric (Part 5.5).
14. ApprovalMentor signs; module counts toward Gate 30. Authority remains A0.

6.3 Sample module M-L6-02: Nmap: safe, authorised network discovery

M-L6-02 · Level 6 · Security Tools · Lab-only until engagement-authorised (T1/T2)
1. DefinitionNmap is a free network scanner that discovers hosts and reports open ports and services. It sends packets to the target; therefore it is an active tool.
2. Business purposeShows the client what is exposed to a network so unnecessary services can be closed and firewall rules verified.
3. Threat / riskUnknown or forgotten services, misconfigured firewalls, shadow systems.
4. PrerequisitesM-L1 TCP/IP and ports; M-L3 firewalls; policy acknowledgement; for any non-lab target, a signed authorisation and A2 authority (T2).
5. Tool installationOfficial project: nmap.org. Ubuntu: sudo apt install -y nmap. Record version with nmap --version. Licence: Nmap Public Source License (check terms for redistribution).
6. Legal & operational impactScanning someone else's network without permission may be illegal in your jurisdiction. Scans can trigger alarms, fill logs, and occasionally crash fragile devices. Use rate limits and agreed windows.
7. Procedure (lab)
  1. Confirm the target IP is in your Lab Authorisation Record and is a VEL lab VM.
  2. Host discovery on the lab subnet only: nmap -sn 192.168.56.0/24
  3. Top-port scan with service versions: nmap -sV --top-ports 1000 -oA lab01-baseline 192.168.56.101
  4. Compare scans before and after hardening using the saved .nmap files.
  5. For firewalled targets, add --max-retries 1 to avoid long waits.
8. Expected outputBefore hardening: SSH plus any lab services listed as open. After hardening: only the intended ports open; others filtered.
9. VerificationCross-check with ss -tulpn on the target. Anything Nmap reports but the host does not list is investigated (NAT, firewall, container).
10. Common mistakesScanning the whole home or office LAN; typing a wrong subnet; scanning a public IP "to test"; running aggressive scripts without approval; forgetting to save output.
11. DocumentationCommand, version, time, target, output files (hash), person, approval reference.
12. Practical assignmentWrite a one-page "scan plan" for the lab (targets, settings, impact, stop conditions), have it approved, then execute and report.
13. AssessmentExplain the impact of -sn, -sV and --top-ports; identify out-of-scope IPs in a sample list.
14. ApprovalSecurity Lead approval of the scan plan for each non-lab use; Tier follows Part 3.

6.4 Sample module M-L6-05: Secret scanning with Gitleaks

M-L6-05 · Level 6 · Dependency and secret scanning · Lab (Project 5) then Tier 1
1. DefinitionGitleaks searches files and Git history for strings that look like passwords, API keys or tokens.
2. Business purposeLeaked credentials let outsiders sign in as the company. Finding them early lets the client revoke them.
3. Threat / riskHard-coded cloud keys, database passwords and tokens committed to repositories, including old commits.
4. PrerequisitesGit basics; M-L4 authentication concepts; for client repositories: authorisation naming the repositories and a read-only clone.
5. Tool installationOfficial project: github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks (releases or package manager). MIT licence. Record version with gitleaks version.
6. Safe configurationRun on a local read-only clone. Use --redact so reports do not store full secrets. Never paste real secrets in tickets or chat.
7. Procedure
  1. Create a training repo with fake secrets only. For example, AWS's documented example key AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE in a file, committed, then deleted in a later commit.
  2. Scan including history: gitleaks detect --source . --redact --report-format json --report-path gitleaks-report.json
  3. Newer versions also provide gitleaks git and gitleaks dir; check gitleaks --help for your version.
  4. Review each hit: real secret, example, or false positive? Record the decision.
  5. Recommend: revoke and rotate the credential, remove from code, use a secrets manager, add a pre-commit scan.
8. Expected outputA report listing rule ID, file, commit and line, with the secret value redacted.
9. VerificationDelete the fake key from the current file: the history scan still finds it in the old commit. This shows why rotation matters more than deletion.
10. Common mistakesBelieving deletion fixes a leak; sharing the unredacted report; ignoring false positives without a recorded reason; testing a real secret to "see if it works" (this is unauthorised access).
11. DocumentationFinding record with commit hash, location, status (confirmed/false positive), recommended action; reports kept in restricted store.
12. Practical assignmentScan the training repo, triage ten hits, write a one-page remediation plan including a pre-commit hook configuration.
13. AssessmentWhy can a "deleted" secret still be dangerous? What must never be done with a discovered credential?
14. ApprovalLab: mentor sign-off. Client repos: Security Lead confirms the repository is named in scope (T1).
Never validate a discovered credential

Do not try a found key or password against a live system to see whether it works, unless the RoE explicitly permits that exact check. Report it, recommend revocation, and let the owner decide.

7.3 Repository and documentation structure

cybersecurity-project/
├── README.md

Never commit sensitive material

Passwords, tokens, customer data, raw scanner output with exploitable detail, and unsanitised evidence do not go into an ordinary Git repository. They live in the approved, restricted-access, encrypted evidence store. The repository holds only sanitised documents and references. Add secret scanning and a pre-commit hook to every project repository.

RatingScore bandCVSS band (guide)Suggested remediation targetApproval
Critical16–259.0–10.07 days, interim mitigation immediatelyLead + second reviewer
High10–157.0–8.930 daysLead + second reviewer
Medium5–94.0–6.990 daysConsultant
Low1–40.1–3.9180 days or next cycleConsultant

Targets are suggested defaults; the client's risk appetite and contract prevail. Scanner alerts are labelled unconfirmed until manually verified (where safe) or confirmed from configuration evidence.

7.5 Final report outline

  1. Executive summary: overall posture, top risks, decisions needed; no exploit detail.
  2. Scope, authorisation reference and limitations (what was not tested).
  3. Methodology and tools (with versions) and standards used (OWASP WSTG, CIS, NIST).
  4. Assets assessed and risk summary chart.
  5. Findings by severity, using the record in 7.4.
  6. Business impact and risk ratings explained.
  7. Remediation plan with owners, dates and quick wins.
  8. Retest status and residual risk.
  9. Restricted technical annex (need-to-know), evidence index.
Honest limitations

State the testing window, access level, excluded systems and the fact that an assessment is a point-in-time sample. Never claim the client is "secure" or "compliant". Say what was found, what was fixed and what remains.

7.6 Managed security: what is and is not included

Typically included (when contracted)Not included unless explicitly agreed
  • Vulnerability tracking and monthly rescans (T1/T2 per RoE)
  • Patch verification and configuration checks
  • Alert triage within stated business hours
  • Quarterly access reviews
  • Incident coordination and evidence guidance
  • Monthly security report; periodic reassessment
  • 24/7 monitoring (only if staffed and tooled to deliver it)
  • Hands-on forensic investigation or legal advice
  • Regulatory notification decisions
  • Fixing client application code
  • Third-party licence costs and cloud platform costs
  • Certification or independent audit

Pricing, margins and recurring revenue (hours, licences, storage, retests, support) are the subject of Module 3. One-time assessment fees and monthly managed fees are always quoted separately.

Part 8 — Security Incident Response

This part trains employees to respond calmly and consistently. The department supports the client's incident response; it does not make legal decisions and does not take actions outside its contract.

8.1 The six phases

#PhaseGoal and key actionsBeginner's role (A0/A1)
1PreparationContacts list, roles, tools, logging enabled, backups tested, playbooks, training and exercisesKnow the escalation list; join tabletops
2IdentificationDetect and confirm an incident; record time, source, symptoms; assign severityReport immediately; do not investigate alone
3ContainmentLimit spread without destroying evidence: isolate host, disable account, block address, as the client owner approvesObserve; take notes; follow instructions
4EradicationRemove cause: patch, remove malicious access, reset credentials, rebuild from trusted imagesSupport with checklists
5RecoveryRestore services from verified backups; monitor closely; confirm normal operationSupport monitoring and verification
6Lessons learnedBlameless review within 5 working days; update controls, runbooks and trainingContribute observations

8.2 Severity levels (suggested defaults)

LevelDefinitionExamplesVEL response target*Escalate to
SEV-1 CriticalConfirmed compromise of critical systems or personal data; ongoing active attacker; major outageRansomware; data exfiltration confirmedImmediate (within 30 min of awareness)Security Lead, Founder, client emergency contact
SEV-2 HighLikely compromise or serious exposure; limited impact so farCompromised admin account; exposed databaseWithin 1 hourSecurity Lead, client contact
SEV-3 MediumSuspicious activity or policy violation, impact containedMalware on one workstation; repeated failed loginsSame business dayConsultant / SOC
SEV-4 LowMinor event, no evidence of impactBlocked phishing email; scan noiseWithin 2 business daysSOC Analyst

* Applies only within contracted hours. Managed-service contracts must state exact hours; do not promise round-the-clock cover that is not staffed.

8.3 Escalation procedure

  1. Detect and record: note exact time (with time zone), what you saw, which asset, who told you.
  2. Tell your Security Lead at once (phone, then message). Do not wait to be sure.
  3. Assign provisional severity using 8.2; the Security Lead confirms.
  4. Notify the client's authorised contact through the agreed channel; the PM keeps a timeline.
  5. Decide containment with the client system owner. VEL recommends; the owner approves changes on their systems.
  6. Escalate to legal/compliance: the Security Lead alerts the client's legal or compliance contact when personal data, regulated data or third parties may be affected.
  7. Record every action in the incident log; close with a lessons-learned review.

8.4 Evidence preservation

Requirement
☐Do not power off or rebuild an affected system until the owner and Security Lead decide; memory and running state may be needed.
☐Work on copies. Preserve originals; copy logs, images and files to the restricted store.
☐Hash and record. Compute SHA-256 (sha256sum file) when collected; note collector, date/time, time zone and source.
☐Chain of custody: every transfer logged (from, to, when, why). Fields in Appendix C.
☐Time synchronisation: note clock offsets between systems so timelines are reliable.
☐Minimise personal data: collect only what the investigation needs; restrict access.
☐No unauthorised "hack back" or contact with the suspected attacker.

8.5 Client notification responsibilities

VEL doesVEL does not
  • Tell the client's authorised contact promptly and factually
  • Provide timeline, facts known, unknowns, and recommended containment
  • Provide evidence in the agreed format
  • Remind the client to involve legal/compliance and, where applicable, their regulator-facing contact
  • Keep a written record of what was communicated and when
  • Decide whether a breach must be notified to a regulator, customers or the public
  • Contact regulators, media or affected individuals on the client's behalf unless contractually instructed in writing
  • Give legal conclusions or speculate on cause or blame
  • Share incident details with anyone outside the authorised list
For awareness only: notification clocks exist

Some laws and directions set short deadlines, for example CERT-In directions in India (six hours for specified cyber incident types), the DPDP Act, 2023, and GDPR's 72-hour rule for personal data breaches. VEL never decides if or when these apply. The Security Lead alerts the client and their counsel immediately so they can decide in time.

8.6 Incidents during an engagement

  • If you find signs of a real compromise, treat it as a stop-work condition (Part 3.8): stop, preserve what you saw, call the Security Lead.
  • If your testing causes an outage, stop, tell the client emergency contact at once, assist restoration and document honestly. Early honesty is protected.
  • If you encounter unexpected personal data, stop, do not copy it, and report; the data handling agreement governs next steps.

8.7 Tabletop exercise 01 (Training Week 8)

Scenario (fictional): a small accounting firm reports that three staff cannot open files and a note demands payment. One staff member says they clicked a link yesterday.

#Questions the group must answer
1What do we know, and what do we not know? What is the provisional severity and why?
2Whom do we tell first, second and third? Who approves containment?
3What evidence must be preserved before any action, and who may touch the machines?
4Which backups exist, and how would we verify them before restoring?
5What do we say to the client contact, and what must we not say (legal decisions, blame, payment advice)?
6What lessons and control changes would we recommend afterwards?

Scoring: participants are assessed on following escalation, evidence discipline, clear communication and respecting limits (Part 5.5).

Part 9 — Lab 01: Isolated Linux Server Hardening Lab

Lab IDLAB-01 · Training Project 1 · Roadmap Week 4 · Level 2
EnvironmentVEL-owned virtual machines on a host-only network. No client systems. No internet-exposed services.
Authority requiredA0 (trainee) with a signed Lab Authorisation Record
Estimated time12–16 hours over 5 days
Approval to completeMentor review, QA Reviewer check of report, Security Lead sign-off (Gate 30)
Lab rule

Every IP address you scan, probe or log in to in this lab must be one of your own lab VMs, listed in your Lab Authorisation Record. If a command could reach any other address, stop and ask.

9.1 Objectives and learning outcomes

  • Build an isolated lab and prove that it is isolated.
  • Capture a baseline of a default Linux server and identify its weaknesses.
  • Apply ten hardening controls safely, with backups, verification and rollback.
  • Compare before and after results and write an evidence-based hardening report.
  • Practise the habit: authorise, snapshot, change, verify, document.

9.2 Lab topology

   Your approved workstation (host)
   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │  Hypervisor (VirtualBox / VMware / KVM)                      │
   │                                                              │
   │   host-only network 192.168.56.0/24  (no route to Internet)  │
   │   ─────────────┬──────────────────────────┬─────────────     │
   │         ┌──────┴───────┐          ┌───────┴──────┐           │
   │         │ lab01-analyst│          │ lab01-target │           │
   │         │ 192.168.56.10│          │192.168.56.101│           │
   │         │ nmap, ssh    │ ───────▶ │ Ubuntu Server│           │
   │         └──────────────┘          │ LTS (hardened)│          │
   │                                   └──────────────┘           │
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   Temporary: a NAT adapter on lab01-target only for package updates,
   then REMOVED (Phase A step 5).

Addresses are examples. VirtualBox's default host-only range is 192.168.56.0/24; use your hypervisor's real values and put your addresses in the Lab Authorisation Record.

VMSpecificationPurpose
lab01-targetUbuntu Server LTS (current supported release), 2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, 20 GB disk, OpenSSH installed during setupThe server you will harden
lab01-analystUbuntu Server or Desktop LTS, 1–2 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, with nmap and sshPlays the role of an outside observer on the lab network

9.3 Prerequisites and tool register

  • Week 1 sign-off complete (legal quiz 100%, POL-SEC-001 signed).
  • Modules L1-01 to L1-06 and L2-01 to L2-04 studied.
  • Free software only. Record each tool, version, source and licence in the tool register: hypervisor, Ubuntu Server LTS, OpenSSH, UFW, fail2ban, auditd, nmap, optional Lynis.

9.4 Phase A: Authorise and isolate (Day 1)

  1. Sign the Lab Authorisation Record (Appendix C) listing VM names, IPs, purpose and dates. The Security Lead countersigns.
  2. Create the host-only network in your hypervisor. Do not choose "bridged" for any lab VM.
  3. Install lab01-target and lab01-analyst. Create an admin user labadmin (not root); install OpenSSH server when asked.
  4. Update the target while the temporary NAT adapter is attached: 
    sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot
  5. Remove the NAT adapter from lab01-target (VM powered off, then in the hypervisor network settings). Boot the VM.
  6. Prove isolation on lab01-target: 
    ip -br addr                 # only the host-only address (e.g. 192.168.56.101)
ip route                    # no default route
ping -c 2 -W 2 1.1.1.1      # must FAIL (network unreachable / 100% loss)
ping -c 2 192.168.56.10     # must succeed (analyst VM)
  7. Take snapshot "S0-clean-isolated" of both VMs.
Isolation check passed only if the target cannot reach the Internet and no lab VM is bridged to your LAN.

9.5 Phase B: Baseline (Day 2)

Record the "before" state. Save outputs to lab01/evidence/baseline/ on your workstation (no real data; safe to store in the training repo).

  1. Configuration backup on the target: 
    sudo tar czf /var/backups/etc-baseline-$(date +%F).tgz /etc
sha256sum /var/backups/etc-baseline-*.tgz | tee ~/etc-baseline.sha256
  2. System facts: 
    lsb_release -a; uname -r; ssh -V
getent passwd | awk -F: '$7 !~ /(nologin|false)$/ {print $1,$7}'
sudo awk -F: '($2==""){print $1}' /etc/shadow
sudo ss -tulpn
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|maxauthtries|x11forwarding|logingracetime)'
sudo ufw status verbose
  3. External view from lab01-analyst (own lab IP only): 
    nmap -sV --top-ports 1000 -oA ~/lab01-baseline 192.168.56.101
  4. Optional audit score. On the target: 
    sudo apt install -y lynis    # temporary NAT needed, or use an offline package
sudo lynis audit system
    Note the "Hardening index" and warnings. The audit is read-only.
  5. Write down weaknesses you see (for example: password login enabled, no firewall, unnecessary services) as draft findings with a likelihood and impact rating (Part 7.4).
  6. Snapshot "S1-baseline".

If the target has no internet, install packages needed for later steps (ufw fail2ban auditd libpam-pwquality unattended-upgrades lynis) before removing the NAT adapter, or reattach NAT briefly; remove it again and re-run the isolation check.

9.6 Phase C: Hardening controls H1–H10 (Days 2–4)

Safety rules for every step
  • Keep a second console session (hypervisor console) open when you change SSH or the firewall.
  • Change one control at a time, verify, then record in the change log.
  • If anything breaks, revert the snapshot or the specific file, and note why.

H1 · Patching and automatic security updates

sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades      # choose Yes
sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug | tail -n 5

Why: known vulnerabilities are the easiest way in. Verify: systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades returns enabled; the dry run completes without errors. Rollback: sudo apt remove unattended-upgrades.

H2 · Accounts and password quality

sudo passwd -l root                                   # lock the root password (sudo still works)
sudo apt install -y libpam-pwquality
sudo sed -i 's/^# *minlen.*/minlen = 14/' /etc/security/pwquality.conf
grep -E '^minlen' /etc/security/pwquality.conf
sudo awk -F: '($2==""){print $1}' /etc/shadow         # expect no output

Why: limits shared or guessable credentials. Verify: sudo passwd -S root shows L (locked); no accounts with empty passwords. Decision log: list each remaining login-capable account with owner and purpose; remove or lock any without one.

H3 · SSH: key login only, no root, limited attempts

On lab01-analyst create a key and copy it:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "lab01-analyst"
ssh-copy-id labadmin@192.168.56.101
ssh labadmin@192.168.56.101        # must log in with the key

On lab01-target create the drop-in file (it must sort before cloud-init files, because the first value wins):

sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-vel-hardening.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
X11Forwarding no
AllowUsers labadmin
EOF
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh

Verify (from analyst): ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no labadmin@192.168.56.101 must give Permission denied (publickey). On target: sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|maxauthtries|allowusers)'. Rollback: sudo rm /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-vel-hardening.conf && sudo systemctl reload ssh (use the hypervisor console if SSH is locked).

H4 · Host firewall (UFW), default deny

sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing
sudo ufw allow from 192.168.56.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp
sudo ufw logging on
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

Always add the SSH allow rule before enabling. Verify: status shows Status: active, default deny (incoming), and port 22 allowed from the lab subnet. Rollback: sudo ufw disable.

H5 · Reduce attack surface

sudo ss -tulpn                                         # what listens?
systemctl list-unit-files --type=service --state=enabled
# Only after confirming a service is unneeded and recording the decision:
sudo systemctl disable --now <service-name>

Why: every listening service is a possible weakness. Verify: only SSH (port 22) listens on the lab address, apart from local-only services such as the system resolver on 127.0.0.53. Never disable a service you cannot explain.

H6 · Brute-force protection (fail2ban)

sudo apt install -y fail2ban
sudo tee /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/vel-sshd.local >/dev/null <<'EOF'
[sshd]
enabled  = true
backend  = systemd
maxretry = 4
findtime = 10m
bantime  = 1h
EOF
sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

Verify: the jail sshd is listed and active. Optional, own lab only: from the analyst VM, try logging in as a non-existent user a few times (ssh nosuchuser@192.168.56.101); check sudo fail2ban-client status sshd for a banned address, then unban with sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 192.168.56.10.

H7 · Audit logging (auditd)

sudo apt install -y auditd
sudo tee /etc/audit/rules.d/vel-lab01.rules >/dev/null <<'EOF'
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers
-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k sudoers
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config -p wa -k sshd
-w /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ -p wa -k sshd
EOF
sudo augenrules --load
sudo auditctl -l

Verify: create and remove a harmless file sudo touch /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/zz-test.conf; sudo rm /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/zz-test.conf, then sudo ausearch -k sshd -ts recent shows the events. Why: you cannot investigate what you did not log.

H8 · Time synchronisation and kernel network settings

timedatectl                                            # System clock synchronized: yes
sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-vel-lab01.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2
EOF
sudo sysctl --system | tail -n 5

Verify: sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies kernel.randomize_va_space returns the values set. Note: accurate time makes logs trustworthy. Without the NAT adapter, time sync may need the hypervisor's guest tools or a lab NTP source; record what you used.

H9 · File permissions and privileged programmes

ls -l /etc/shadow /etc/passwd /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -ls 2>/dev/null       # world-writable files
sudo find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f -ls 2>/dev/null      # setuid programmes (review only)
chmod 700 ~/.ssh && chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys

Verify: no unexpected world-writable files; each setuid programme is a normal system component you can explain. Do not remove setuid bits you do not understand; note them as questions for your mentor.

H10 · Backup and configuration baseline

sudo tar czf /var/backups/etc-hardened-$(date +%F).tgz /etc
sudo sha256sum /var/backups/etc-hardened-*.tgz | tee ~/etc-hardened.sha256

Verify: extract both archives into separate folders and run diff -ru baseline/etc hardened/etc; every difference corresponds to a change-log entry. Take snapshot "S2-hardened". Proof of rollback: restore S1-baseline, confirm the weak settings are back, then restore S2.



9.7 Phase D: Verify and compare (Day 5)


    

  1. Repeat all baseline commands from 9.5 and save to evidence/after/.
    2. 

  2. From lab01-analyst scan again (own lab IP only): 
    nmap -sV --top-ports 1000 --max-retries 1 -oA ~/lab01-after 192.168.56.101
     Expected: 22/tcp open (OpenSSH); everything else filtered or closed.
    3. 

  3. Compare scans: ndiff ~/lab01-baseline.xml ~/lab01-after.xml (installed with Nmap).
    4. 

  4. Re-run Lynis if used; record the new hardening index and remaining suggestions.
    5. 

  5. Run a functionality check: legitimate admin login by key works; updates install; logs are written; time is synchronised.
    6.

9.8 Common mistakes and troubleshooting




SymptomLikely cause / fix



Cannot SSH after H3Key not copied or AllowUsers wrong. Use the hypervisor console, remove the drop-in, reload, repeat step by step.


sshd -T still shows passwordauthentication yesAnother file set it first. List /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/; your file must sort earlier (e.g. 10-).


Locked out after enabling UFWSSH allow rule missing or wrong subnet. Console: sudo ufw allow from 192.168.56.0/24 to any port 22 proto tcp.


Nmap scan is very slow after the firewallDropped packets cause retries. Use --top-ports 1000 --max-retries 1.


Packages fail to installNo network (NAT removed). Install needed packages first, or briefly re-attach NAT and re-check isolation.


fail2ban shows no jailCheck /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/vel-sshd.local spelling and sudo journalctl -u fail2ban -n 30.


Scanned an IP not in your recordStop. Report to the Security Lead immediately (Part 3.11).

TermMeaning



AssetAnything of value to protect: system, data, application, account, process

Appendix D: Beginner quick-reference card




Before I run anything, I ask…If the answer is "no" or "not sure"



Is this target in my signed authorisation or Lab record?Stop. Do not run it.


Is today and now inside the permitted window?Stop.


Does my authority level allow this tier?Ask the Security Lead.


Do I know what traffic this will send and what it could break?Read the module; ask the mentor.


Have I backed up and can I roll back?Take the snapshot or backup first.


Where will the output be stored, and does it contain secrets?Use the restricted store; redact.
